Allocating plant area by measured flow (option C) assumes the answer being tested. Installed area (option D) can include area that is not active. Course convention: installed and active area are distinguished in this module.

checks.prompt: Fictional study assumptions: a verified filtration totalizer increases by 900 m³ over 5 h, with no reset or missing endpoints. What does dividing these values establish?
choices: A maximum filtration flow of 180 m³/h within the recorded interval.
An authorized filtration flow of 180 m³/h for subsequent comparable runs.
A constant filtration flow of 180 m³/h throughout the full interval.
An average filtration flow of 180 m³/h over the recorded interval.
checks.explanation: Volume divided by elapsed time gives an interval average of 900 ÷ 5 = 180 m³/h. It is not a maximum (option A), since flow could have been higher at times. It is not an authorized flow (option C). It does not show constant flow (option D), because endpoints cannot reveal variation within the interval. Source: sp6 section 5.6.8.1, Flow Rate through a Filter (p. 119).

checks.prompt: Why should a study comparison state whether run age begins at backwash completion, filtration restart or return to the treated-water stream?
choices: Those events can occur at different times and change the assigned run stage.
Those events allow recovery records to replace missing established-run records.
Those events determine hydraulic loading without an individual flow record.
Those events identify equivalent times once the historian stores the readings.
checks.explanation: These events need not coincide, so the chosen origin changes the run stage assigned to each reading. Recovery records cannot replace established-run records (option A). Run age does not determine loading (option B), which needs flow and area. Storing readings in the historian does not make the events equivalent (option D). Source: sp6 section 5.6.8.3, Unit Filter Run Volume (p. 121).

checks.prompt: In a fictional study record, combined filtered-water turbidity remains steady while a lower-flow filter shows a brief rise. Which interpretation is supported?
choices: The combined trace establishes stable performance for each contributing unit.
The combined trace may mask the event through blending and sampling timing.
The individual trace establishes a corresponding rise at the combined point.
The combined trace invalidates the individual result because mixing is complete.
checks.explanation: Blending and sampling delay can hide a short rise from a lower-flow unit. A steady combined trace (option A) cannot show that each unit is stable. A rise at one filter (option B) does not automatically appear at the combined point. Complete mixing (option C) does not invalidate the individual result. Course convention: the combined-versus-individual distinction in this module.

checks.prompt: Fictional study records show a turbidity rise after a flow increase, but sample-line condition and clock alignment remain unchecked. Which statement keeps observation separate from explanation?
choices: The sequence excludes an upstream contribution because the local flow changed first.
The recorded rise identifies a sample disturbance rather than a treatment change.
The recorded rise followed the increase; causation still needs supporting evidence.
The sequence confirms that increased loading caused the observed breakthrough.
checks.explanation: The timing is an observation, and attributing it to loading is a hypothesis. Ordering alone does not exclude an upstream cause (option B). Naming a sample disturbance (option C) asserts a cause the records do not yet support. Stating that loading caused breakthrough (option D) treats sequence as proof. Course convention: observation and explanation are kept separate in this module.

checks.prompt: What can an individual-filter turbidity reading contribute to a training assessment of treatment performance?
choices: It establishes treatment credit when the combined filtered-water trace is stable.
It demonstrates overall disinfection adequacy when paired with verified loading records.
It supplies a direct pathogen count for calculating the unit's removal efficiency.
It provides performance evidence but does not independently establish removal credit.
checks.explanation: A reading is performance evidence but does not establish removal credit. A stable combined trace (option A) does not establish credit for a unit. Loading records (option C) do not demonstrate disinfection adequacy, which depends on CT. Turbidity gives no direct pathogen count (option D). Source: Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario).

modules.title: Check disinfection calculations and their limits
objectives: Calculate CT from a defined residual and effective contact time.
Distinguish nominal detention time from T10.
Evaluate changing flow, level and chemistry against a supplied criterion.
modules.lesson: ### Define the calculation before using it This module is study and training material for a non-credit pilot. It is not operating or compliance instruction. All facilities, operators, records and readings are fictional. Every numerical process value and comparison criterion is a supplied case assumption, not an authorized operating value. CT combines a disinfectant concentration with an effective contact time. In the simplified relationship used here, CT = C × T10, with C in mg/L and T10 in minutes, giving CT in mg·min/L. The multiplication is simple. Establishing that the concentration, time and criterion belong together is the difficult part. The Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario) explains the CT concept, T10 and disinfectant-specific treatment requirements. Use it to understand the framework. A real assessment also needs the facility's approval, approved disinfection basis and validated calculation procedure. Before calculating, define the question. Which disinfectant species is assessed? Which organism and treatment objective apply? Where does the segment begin and end? Is the residual measured where the method requires? What temperature, pH and hydraulic configuration apply? Dose is not residual. Dose is the disinfectant introduced; residual is what remains after reactions and decay. Substituting feed dose for residual overstates available disinfection. Total chlorine and free chlorine are different measurements, and a free-chlorine calculation cannot accept a total-chlorine reading merely because both are shown in mg/L. A CT ratio is the assessed CT divided by the applicable criterion. A ratio above 1.0 means the calculated value exceeds the criterion under the stated assumptions. It does not independently prove compliance. Unsupported hydraulic assumptions, an unsuitable criterion or unreliable residual data can invalidate a correct arithmetic result. ### Build an input register and establish effective time Nominal detention time is working volume divided by flow through the segment. It describes a volume-to-flow relationship, not the actual distribution of travel times. Mixing, short-circuiting, dead zones and inlet or outlet arrangements can cause some water to leave much earlier than the nominal time suggests. T10 is the travel time by which about ten percent of a tracer has passed the outlet. The ten percent defines a hydraulic statistic; it is not an operating limit. The tracer interpretation must come from the accepted hydraulic assessment. Course convention: the examples treat the T10 relationship as a supplied factor of nominal time, the baffling factor. Do not assume a constant factor because a spreadsheet has a cell for one. A factor supported at one configuration may be unsupported with a compartment isolated or a bypass open. | Input | Record to consult | Reason to question or reject the input | |---|---|---| | Residual | Specified analyser channel, method and QC record | Wrong species, stale value or failed check | | Residual location | Approved segment drawing and sample point | Sample is upstream of the required endpoint | | Working volume | Level record and validated level-volume relationship | Nameplate capacity replaces actual water volume | | Effective-time basis | Accepted tracer report or authorized hydraulic basis | Current flow, level or valve arrangement is outside its scope | For parallel branches, identify the flow and volume of the branch being assessed. Dividing combined tank volume by total flow can conceal a poorly performing branch. Time alignment also matters: an analyser may receive water through a sample line with transport delay, so its display describes water sampled earlier. Use the validated alignment method rather than an invented shift. ### Worked example: calculate a supported baseline All values are supplied assumptions for a fictional contactor. The case specifies a free-chlorine residual of 0.90 mg/L, a working volume of 600 m³, a segment flow of 360 m³/h and a supported factor of 0.40 for this steady condition. Temperature is 12 °C and pH is 7.2. The supplied CT criterion for this disinfectant, chemistry and objective is 30 mg·min/L. It is for arithmetic practice only and must not be reused elsewhere. **Step 1:** Q = 360 m³/h ÷ 60 min/h = 6.00 m³/min. **Step 2:** nominal time = 600 m³ ÷ 6.00 m³/min = 100 min. This is not yet effective contact time. **Step 3:** T10 = 100 min × 0.40 = 40.0 min. **Step 4:** CT = 0.90 mg/L × 40.0 min = 36.0 mg·min/L. **Step 5:** CT ratio = 36.0 ÷ 30 = 1.20. CT difference = 36.0 − 30 = 6.0 mg·min/L. **Answer:** the fictional baseline CT is 36.0 mg·min/L, with a ratio of 1.20. The margin is a calculated result under the case assumptions. It is not permission to reduce chemical feed or increase production. The uncertainty in residual, volume and the hydraulic factor has not been established. Record which values were measured, derived and assumed. ### Worked example: reassess changed flow, level and chemistry The case now has a stable working volume of 540 m³ and a segment flow of 450 m³/h. Residual remains 0.90 mg/L. The fictional hydraulic assessment supports the same factor of 0.40 at this second stable condition. That support is an assumption of the example, not a general claim that factors stay constant. **Step 1:** Q = 450 ÷ 60 = 7.50 m³/min. **Step 2:** nominal time = 540 ÷ 7.50 = 72.0 min. **Step 3:** T10 = 72.0 × 0.40 = 28.8 min. **Step 4:** CT = 0.90 × 28.8 = 25.92 mg·min/L. **Step 5:** CT ratio = 25.92 ÷ 30 = 0.864. CT shortfall = 30 − 25.92 = 4.08 mg·min/L. **Answer:** CT is below the criterion. The unchanged residual has not preserved CT, because effective contact time fell. Now consider a chemistry variant at the same hydraulic condition: temperature 6 °C, pH 7.6 and a new criterion of 36 mg·min/L. The assessed CT is still 25.92 mg·min/L, but the ratio is 25.92 ÷ 36 = 0.720. The criterion changed although the multiplication inputs did not. Temperature and pH affect disinfectants differently. Do not transfer a free-chlorine interpretation to another disinfectant. ### Judge validity and prepare a controlled trial record Separate three questions: is the arithmetic correct, are the inputs supported, and is the criterion applicable? A correct answer to the first cannot compensate for a failure in the other two. During a sudden flow or level change, water already in the contactor has experienced an earlier condition. A steady-state calculation may not describe the water history. Use the validated transient method where one exists, or label the result unsupported. A flat residual trend could mean stable treatment, or a frozen analyser output during maintenance. Check instrument status, sample flow, maintenance entries and quality flags. The US EPA publication Generating high-quality turbidity data (EPA 815-B-19-010) is United States technical guidance, not Ontario law. It supports checking the measurement chain, but it does not validate a chlorine analyser or an Ontario CT method. State conclusions narrowly. A defensible statement says that a specified calculation exceeds or falls below a criterion under listed assumptions. It should not be labelled a pass because an optimistic input produces a favourable ratio. ### Common errors - **Using tank capacity instead of working volume.** Nameplate capacity overstates detention time when the level is lower. - **Using nominal time as T10.** Omitting the supported hydraulic factor overstates effective time. - **Mixing favourable readings from different intervals.** A high residual from one period and low flow from another may never have existed together. - **Treating every chlorine result as interchangeable.** Free chlorine, total chlorine and dose answer different questions. - **Keeping the old criterion after chemistry changes.** Correct multiplication does not validate an unsuitable criterion. ### What to verify before you act Consult the facility's Municipal Drinking Water Licence and Drinking Water Works Permit, and identify the conditions that govern the disinfection assessment. Check the Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario) with the facility's approved design basis and validated CT procedure. Confirm the tracer study or hydraulic assessment covers the actual flow, level, compartment arrangement and valve status. Review flowmeter verification, analyser quality-control records, temperature and pH data, and historian status. Before any optimization trial or operational response, consult the authorized trial plan and the escalation records. If an input or criterion cannot be substantiated, the calculation is not decision-ready.
modules.evidence:
### Fictional worked scenario: reject an unsupported hydraulic factor

The facility, operators, records and readings in this scenario are fictional. Every process value and criterion is a supplied training assumption, not an authorized operating value. This exercise supports a non-credit pilot and is not operating or compliance instruction.

The fictional Maple Reach contactor has a baseline working volume of 480 m³ and segment flow of 240 m³/h. Its specified endpoint free-chlorine residual is 0.75 mg/L. Temperature is 12 °C and pH is 7.2, dimensionless. The case supplies a CT criterion of 28 mg·min/L for its stated treatment objective and chemistry.

The controlled case hydraulic report supports a dimensionless factor of 0.35 at both conditions assessed below. An unsigned spreadsheet instead uses a dimensionless factor of 0.60, with no tracer reference. Reject that spreadsheet factor. A separate total-chlorine reading of 0.95 mg/L is also unsuitable for this free-chlorine calculation.

Baseline arithmetic:

- Q = 240 m³/h × 1 h/60 min = 4.00 m³/min.
- t_nominal = 480 m³ ÷ 4.00 m³/min = 120 min.
- T10 = 120 min × 0.35 dimensionless = 42.0 min.
- CT = 0.75 mg/L × 42.0 min = 31.5 mg·min/L.
- Ratio = 31.5 mg·min/L ÷ 28 mg·min/L = 1.125 dimensionless.

A later stable interval has a supplied working volume of 420 m³ and flow of 300 m³/h. Residual and chemistry are unchanged.

- Q = 300 m³/h × 1 h/60 min = 5.00 m³/min.
- t_nominal = 420 m³ ÷ 5.00 m³/min = 84.0 min.
- T10 = 84.0 min × 0.35 dimensionless = 29.4 min.
- CT = 0.75 mg/L × 29.4 min = 22.05 mg·min/L.
- Ratio = 22.05 mg·min/L ÷ 28 mg·min/L = 0.7875 dimensionless.

**Answer:** the baseline exceeds the supplied criterion; the later interval falls below it. Retain aligned raw records, hydraulic support, chemistry evidence and the rejected spreadsheet with reasons. The Ontario source, *Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario)*, informs the CT and T10 concepts, not these fictional numerical criteria.
modules.assignment: Prepare a two-column calculation for the lesson's two intervals: 600 m³ at 360 m³/h (baseline, residual 0.90 mg/L, factor 0.40) and 540 m³ at 450 m³/h (changed flow). For each interval show nominal time, T10, CT and CT ratio, with units on every line. Write an input-verification checklist and explain why a stable residual does not demonstrate an unchanged disinfection margin. Then identify two facts needed before transferring this calculation to a real treatment segment.
rubric: Obtains 100 min nominal time, 40.0 min T10, CT of 36.0 mg·min/L and ratio 1.20 for the baseline, and 72.0 min, 28.8 min, 25.92 mg·min/L and ratio 0.864 after the change.
Uses minutes consistently and distinguishes dose, residual, nominal time and effective contact time.
Treats the supplied CT criterion and factor as fictional exercise inputs, and identifies the real validation and chemistry evidence needed.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Have the learner recompute at a lower working volume to demonstrate sensitivity. Accept a clear below-criterion conclusion for the exercise without a plant operating prescription. Reject arbitrary selection of a different required CT merely to make the ratio exceed one.

Analyse the supplied evidence, complete the written assignment and check units, timestamps and assumptions.

checks.prompt: In a fictional training case, the calculation method specifies endpoint free-chlorine residual. Which input belongs in the concentration term?
choices: The verified free-chlorine residual at the endpoint.
The total-chlorine residual from the endpoint analyser.
The free-chlorine residual measured before the contactor.
The chlorine feed dose recorded at the dosing point.
checks.explanation: The concentration term is the verified free-chlorine residual at the specified endpoint. Total chlorine (option B) is a different species. A residual measured before the contactor (option C) is the wrong location. Feed dose (option D) is disinfectant added, not residual remaining after reactions and decay. Source: sp6 section 5.6.9.3, Calculating Chlorine Dose, Demand, and Residual (p. 126); Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario).

checks.prompt: In an accepted tracer interpretation, what does T10 describe?
choices: The elapsed time at which the disinfectant residual is first measured at the outlet.
The travel time by which approximately ten percent of tracer has passed the outlet.
The first arrival time of any tracer at the outlet, before any percentage is applied.
The average travel time calculated from working volume and flow.
checks.explanation: T10 is the travel time by which about ten percent of tracer has passed the outlet. Option A confuses a residual measurement time with a tracer statistic. Option C gives first arrival, which is earlier than any defined percentile. Option D gives nominal detention time, volume divided by flow, which ignores the tracer distribution. Source: Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario), T10 concept.

checks.prompt: Fictional supplied case assumptions are an endpoint free-chlorine residual of 0.80 mg/L and a supported T10 of 25 min. Using CT = C × T10, what is CT?
choices: The calculated CT is 2.0 mg·min/L.
The calculated CT is 31.25 mg·min/L.
The calculated CT is 20.0 mg·min/L.
The calculated CT is 0.032 mg·min/L.
checks.explanation: CT = 0.80 mg/L × 25 min = 20.0 mg·min/L. The 2.0 answer comes from multiplying by 2.5 instead of 25. The 31.25 answer divides time by residual, which is not the CT relationship. The 0.032 answer divides residual by time. Source: sp6 section 5.6.9.3 (p. 126); Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario).

checks.prompt: A fictional input register lists tank nameplate capacity as working volume, although the contactor level varies. Which record best supports the volume input?
choices: The previous shift's volume estimate from its operating log.
The design report's nominal volume at the original design level.
The tank drawing showing its maximum storage capacity.
The current level and validated level-volume relationship.
checks.explanation: The current level converted through the validated level-volume relationship gives the water actually present. A previous shift's estimate (option A) may be stale. A nominal design volume (option B) assumes the design level. A drawing of maximum capacity (option C) is nameplate capacity, which can overstate the water present. Source: sp6 section 5.6.7.2, Detention Time (p. 114).

checks.prompt: A fictional calculation exceeds its supplied, condition-matched CT criterion. What does that comparison establish by itself?
choices: The assessed CT exceeds that criterion under the stated assumptions.
The treatment train satisfies the disinfection and filtration obligations.
The assessed segment can accept increased flow without another review.
The residual target can be reduced by the same proportion as the CT margin.
checks.explanation: The comparison establishes only the numerical relationship under the stated assumptions. It does not show that every treatment barrier is met (option B), that flow can increase without review (option C), or that the residual target can be lowered (option D). Those conclusions need the approved basis and validated procedure. Source: Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario), CT ratio interpretation.

checks.prompt: A fictional contactor's hydraulic factor was supported with every compartment in service. One compartment is now isolated. What should a training reviewer conclude?
choices: The factor can be scaled directly by the fraction of compartments remaining.
The changed arrangement needs a hydraulic basis within its supported scope.
The original factor remains suitable whenever the plant flow stays below design flow.
The original factor remains suitable if the endpoint residual is unchanged.
checks.explanation: Isolating a compartment changes flow paths, so the original factor may no longer apply. Scaling by compartment count (option A) has no support unless the accepted method provides it. Staying below design flow (option C) does not preserve the flow paths. An unchanged residual (option D) does not validate a changed hydraulic basis. Course convention: the supported-scope rule in this module.

modules.title: Design and defend an optimization trial
objectives: Define success and stop criteria before a trial.
Separate observed improvement from causal attribution.
Prepare a cross-barrier review and handover.
modules.lesson:
### Frame a trial that can answer a specific question

This module is study and training material, not operating or compliance instruction. The pilot is non-credit. Any plant trial requires the facility's authorization and protection framework. All facilities, operators, records and readings are fictional. Numerical criteria and operating values are supplied case assumptions for calculation practice, not authorized values or general requirements.

An optimization trial compares a defined change against a credible baseline while protecting every treatment barrier. Start with a question narrow enough to answer: does a candidate coagulation condition reduce settled-water turbidity under comparable source-water conditions without unacceptable effects on filtration, disinfection or chemical use? A lower settled-water reading answers only part of that question.

Identify the variable being changed and the variables intended to remain stable. If several conditions change together, describe the intervention as a package, and do not claim that one component caused the result unless the comparison can separate its effect.

The baseline must represent the process being compared. Yesterday's best reading is not a baseline. Use the facility's sampling plan to select representative locations, operating states and observation periods, including normal variation rather than only quiet periods. Record source turbidity, temperature, pH, alkalinity where relevant, production flow, filters in service, recent backwashes and instrument status.

Separate three statements in the trial record:

- **Observation:** the measured outcome changed during the candidate interval.
- **Association:** the change occurred while the candidate was in use under documented conditions.
- **Causal interpretation:** the evidence supports the candidate, rather than another changing condition, as the explanation.

A planned return to baseline, where authorized and practicable, helps reveal whether an apparent improvement was a source-water trend. It is not a reason to create unnecessary treatment changes.

### Set acceptance, stop and data-quality criteria in advance

Write decision rules before collecting candidate results. Success criteria describe the evidence needed for further evaluation. Stop criteria identify conditions that require action under the approved trial and response procedures. Data-quality criteria determine whether the evidence can be interpreted at all. A trial can show an attractive average and still fail its protection criteria; invalid measurements can make a trial inconclusive without showing that treatment failed.

| Decision item | Define before the trial | Effect on interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Primary outcome | Sampling location, metric, comparison basis, prospective criterion | Determines whether the proposed benefit was observed |
| Filter protection | Individual-filter measures and interruption criteria | Combined results must not hide a deteriorating filter |
| Disinfection protection | Review using the approved configuration and hydraulic basis | An incomplete review prevents an all-barriers success claim |
| Measurement validity | Checks, allowable data treatment, response to missing data | Failed quality checks can make the comparison inconclusive |

Specify when observations become eligible. An upstream change does not reach every monitoring point at once, so base observation windows on the site's documented process response and hydraulic understanding. Define transient handling, such as startup or backwash recovery, prospectively. Deleting an inconvenient transient after seeing the result is selection bias. Also define what happens when evidence is unavailable: missing evidence is not evidence of safe performance.

An extension needs its own authorization and rationale. Extending only unsuccessful trials until a favourable result appears makes the comparison misleading.

### Worked example: calculate improvement without overstating causation

This fictional example uses supplied case assumptions. Four matched observations represent each condition. The draft study plan defines a reduction of at least 20% in arithmetic mean settled-water turbidity as its primary learning criterion. Course convention: 20% is an illustrative study criterion for this lesson, not an Ontario requirement. Each item in this module states its own criterion, and the criterion in one item should not be carried into another.

| Matched observation | Baseline, NTU | Candidate, NTU |
|---|---:|---:|
| A | 0.80 | 0.60 |
| B | 0.84 | 0.64 |
| C | 0.76 | 0.56 |
| D | 0.80 | 0.60 |

Baseline sum: 0.80 + 0.84 + 0.76 + 0.80 = 3.20 NTU; mean = 3.20 ÷ 4 = 0.80 NTU. Candidate sum: 0.60 + 0.64 + 0.56 + 0.60 = 2.40 NTU; mean = 2.40 ÷ 4 = 0.60 NTU.

Absolute reduction: 0.80 − 0.60 = 0.20 NTU. Relative reduction: 0.20 ÷ 0.80 × 100% = 25%. Margin over the 20% criterion: 5 percentage points.

**Answer:** the candidate mean is 0.60 NTU, an observed reduction of 25%. It meets the supplied learning criterion. It does not, by itself, demonstrate trial success or prove causation.

An arithmetic mean can hide short deterioration. Review the sequence and any peak, duration or variability measure selected in advance. Do not add a new favourable metric after the primary result is known and present it as the original test. Four observations do not establish that the effect persists across seasons, and adjacent high-frequency readings are not independent comparisons. If source turbidity fell during the candidate interval, report the observed reduction, identify the source-water trend and seek a better comparison.

### Worked example: distinguish chemical savings from lower production

Chemical consumption needs a consistent basis. A decrease in kilograms per day can result from treating less water. Compare mass per treated volume, and confirm whether the mass is commercial product, dry material or active-equivalent chemical.

Supplied reconciled records show baseline active-equivalent use of 216 kg/d at 12,000 m³/d, and candidate use of 180 kg/d at 9,000 m³/d.

Baseline: 216 kg/d = 216,000,000 mg/d; 12,000 m³/d = 12,000,000 L/d; dose = 216,000,000 ÷ 12,000,000 = 18 mg/L.

Candidate: 180 kg/d = 180,000,000 mg/d; 9,000 m³/d = 9,000,000 L/d; dose = 180,000,000 ÷ 9,000,000 = 20 mg/L.

Daily mass fell by 36 kg/d, a reduction of 16.7%. Normalized use rose by 2 mg/L, an increase of 11.1%.

**Answer:** daily consumption decreased, but chemical mass per treated volume increased. A claim of improved chemical-use efficiency is unsupported by these figures.

This is a period-average reconciliation, not proof of the instantaneous applied dose. Inventory timing, feed calibration and flow-meter error can all affect it. A partial-day chemical total divided by a full-day flow total is invalid. If performance improved while normalized use rose, describe both the benefit and the trade-off.

### Review every barrier and prepare an evidence-based handover

Follow the changed water through the train. Lower settled-water turbidity may reduce filter solids loading, but it does not ensure better filter performance. Compare similar positions within filter runs and record backwash events, because a freshly washed filter and a late-run filter are not equivalent units. If production flow changes, evaluate its effect on filter loading before attributing the result to coagulation.

Disinfection needs its own aligned review. CT depends on disinfectant, temperature, pH, residual and the approved hydraulic basis (Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water, Ontario). Nominal tank volume divided by flow is not automatically an acceptable T10. A residual from another interval cannot close the trial's disinfection review, and neither can a hydraulic assessment for a different arrangement. Do not assign treatment credit from settled-water improvement alone.

Measurement quality is part of the barrier review. Generating high-quality turbidity data (EPA 815-B-19-010) and Field turbidity measurement are United States technical guidance, not Ontario law. Sample-line delay, bubbles, fouling, maintenance modes, timestamp errors and historian averaging can distort a comparison. A grab sample and an online reading may differ because they represent different water or times, so investigate the mismatch rather than choosing the lower result.

A handover should state the trial status, current condition, process-response stage, outstanding samples, quality concerns and stop criteria. Identify who owns each unresolved check and the approved reversion reference. Close with a bounded conclusion: observed benefit, comparison limitations, barrier findings and the next proposed review. An unresolved downstream record keeps the all-barriers conclusion open.

### Common errors

- **Changing the acceptance rule after seeing the result.** Preserve the original rule and label any added analysis as exploratory.
- **Treating missing or frozen data as stable operation.** Check instrument status and quality flags first.
- **Comparing unmatched process periods.** Different source conditions, flows or run stages can explain an apparent benefit.
- **Calling reduced daily chemical mass an efficiency gain.** Compare mass per treated volume.
- **Using a downstream result from another configuration.** A disinfection review must represent the relevant configuration.

### What to verify before you act

For an actual facility, consult the documents below through the site's authorization process. This lesson does not authorize a trial. Verify the Drinking Water Works Permit, Municipal Drinking Water Licence and approval conditions, and confirm whether the trial is within the authorized configuration. Check the approved trial plan for the proposed variable, acceptance criteria, stop criteria, observation coverage, escalation contacts and reversion procedure. Review sampling and measurement records, including units, location, timestamp convention and quality flags. Verify the disinfection procedure, the approved hydraulic assessment and the time-aligned residual, flow, temperature and pH data. Adverse drinking water test results carry reporting duties; the applicable regulation sets the reporting time, and the site's current reporting procedure sets the recipients and required information. Trial review does not replace these duties.
modules.evidence:
### Fictional worked scenario: defend a limited conclusion

The facility, operators, records and readings in this scenario are fictional. All numerical values and criteria are supplied case assumptions for a non-credit training exercise, not authorized operating values.

Cedar Point's draft study plan defines a primary learning criterion of at least 15% lower arithmetic mean settled-water turbidity, with separate filtration and disinfection reviews required. Eligible baseline readings are 0.70 NTU and 0.90 NTU. Eligible candidate readings are 0.55 NTU and 0.65 NTU. The fictional quality register documents satisfactory measurement checks and comparable source conditions.

The flow historian shows baseline production of 10,000 m³/d and candidate production of 8,000 m³/d. A summary note says, 'Flow unchanged; candidate alone caused improvement; all barriers passed.' Its attached disinfection calculation represents an earlier interval and a different tank configuration. The learner must reject the unsupported conclusions in that note while retaining it in the audit trail.

**Worked solution**

Baseline sum = 0.70 NTU + 0.90 NTU = 1.60 NTU.

Baseline mean = 1.60 NTU ÷ 2 = 0.80 NTU.

Candidate sum = 0.55 NTU + 0.65 NTU = 1.20 NTU.

Candidate mean = 1.20 NTU ÷ 2 = 0.60 NTU.

Absolute reduction = 0.80 NTU − 0.60 NTU = 0.20 NTU.

Relative reduction = (0.20 NTU ÷ 0.80 NTU) × 100% = 25%.

Flow decrease = 10,000 m³/d − 8,000 m³/d = 2,000 m³/d.

Relative flow decrease = (2,000 m³/d ÷ 10,000 m³/d) × 100% = 20%.

**Answer:** the observed 25% reduction meets the supplied primary criterion, but the 20% flow decrease confounds attribution. Overall success remains unproven. Consistent with the **Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario)**, the disinfection review needs condition-specific evidence and the approved hydraulic basis for the actual configuration. Retain the historian export, quality register, conflicting note and calculation. Handover must identify the unresolved filtration and disinfection reviews and refer further action to the authorized trial procedure.
modules.assignment: Using the Cedar Point case in the evidence, produce a trial review containing a normalized dose comparison, a cross-barrier evidence table and a critique of the draft claim. Use the lesson's chemical-use figures (216 kg/d at 12,000 m³/d and 180 kg/d at 9,000 m³/d) for the normalized comparison. Design the next controlled comparison, with baseline, source characterization, response lag, sampling plan, authorization, acceptance criteria and stop and escalation rules. Submit an 800 to 1,200-word protocol and handover with calculations, and defend one alternative explanation in the instructor debrief.
rubric: Calculates 18 and 20 mg/L for the two intervals (216 kg/d ÷ 12,000 m³/d; 180 kg/d ÷ 9,000 m³/d), and shows that the lower mass rate tracks lower flow and does not establish lower chemical use per volume.
Separates the observed settled-water improvement from the flow decrease, and records the disinfection and individual-filter reviews as unresolved.
Provides prospective whole-train criteria, timing, authority and evidence retention, and avoids an unsupported all-barriers success claim.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Expected doses: 216 ÷ 12,000 × 1,000 = 18 mg/L and 180 ÷ 9,000 × 1,000 = 20 mg/L. The efficiency claim is unsupported because mass per treated volume rose. Require a meaningful proposal for aligning conditions and observing the downstream response. Ask what would justify an inconclusive result, and do not reward a learner solely for naming a preferred candidate.

activities.instruction: Study the lesson and reconstruct its worked example without looking at the solution.
Read the indicated source sections. Record the section used and one limitation on applying it to this case.
Analyse the supplied evidence, complete the written assignment and check units, timestamps and assumptions.
Compare one decision with an alternative interpretation, then self-check it against the case evidence and exercise feedback. Optional notes can capture your reasoning; count only active work.
Complete the module checks and final assessment; the course evaluation is optional. Review the automatic case feedback to address remaining questions.

checks.prompt: Non-credit study only, not operating or compliance instruction. When designing an optimization trial, how should success, protection and data-quality criteria relate?
choices: Rank them after the trial according to the strongest measured benefit.
Use protection criteria alone to determine trial success.
Define them separately before candidate observations begin.
Combine them into a single average-performance target.
checks.explanation: Defining success, protection and data-quality criteria separately, before observations begin, keeps benefit, barrier protection and interpretability distinct. Ranking criteria after seeing results (option B) lets favourable outcomes choose the test. Protection criteria alone (option C) cannot show that the intended benefit occurred. A single average target (option D) hides failures in protection or data quality. Course convention: the prospective-criteria rule in this module.

checks.prompt: Which approach provides the most defensible baseline for an optimization trial?
choices: Pool the archived readings without separating operating states or measurement quality.
Choose the recent interval with the lowest settled-water turbidity.
Select the most stable interval from the previous shift.
Use representative intervals selected through the facility's validated sampling plan.
checks.explanation: A baseline should represent the process conditions and variation the sampling plan defines. Pooling readings without separating operating states (option A) mixes unlike conditions. Choosing the lowest recent interval (option C) selects favourable data. Selecting the most stable interval (option D) excludes the normal variation the comparison must represent. Course convention: representative sampling as set out in this module.

checks.prompt: A fictional laboratory screening test improves settled-water turbidity. Which conclusion respects the test's unit of comparison?
choices: The result supports a hypothesis needing full-scale barrier evaluation.
The result demonstrates that full-scale contact hydraulics will remain adequate.
The result justifies replacing the plant baseline.
The result establishes acceptable performance across the treatment train.
checks.explanation: A laboratory screen supports a hypothesis that needs full-scale evaluation. It cannot show full-scale hydraulics (option A), justify replacing the plant baseline (option B), or establish performance across the train (option D), because those outcomes were not measured at full scale. Course convention: the unit-of-comparison rule in this module.

checks.prompt: A fictional trial includes backwash-recovery observations. What is the strongest approach to deciding whether these observations enter the primary comparison?
choices: Exclude recovery observations whenever they increase the candidate mean.
Apply prospective transient rules and retain the documented basis for exclusions.
Include each recovery observation without considering the comparison design.
Retain just recovery observations that resemble the baseline's most stable operating period.
checks.explanation: Prospective transient rules, with the basis for any exclusion documented, stop favourable results from deciding which observations count. Excluding observations because they raise the mean (option A) is selection bias. Including all of them regardless of design (option B) ignores the comparison's purpose. Keeping only observations resembling the most stable period (option C) removes the variation the comparison must test. Course convention: prospective transient rules.

checks.prompt: A fictional trial report shows a lower candidate mean but omits the time sequence. What additional evidence best addresses the limitations of that average?
choices: A recalculated mean after removing the highest candidate observations as outliers.
The total number of readings collected during each condition.
The raw sequence and the prospectively selected deterioration measures.
The lowest candidate value and its corresponding timestamp.
checks.explanation: The raw sequence and the prespecified peak, duration or variability measures reveal deterioration that an average hides. A mean after trimming the highest observations (option B) removes the evidence of deterioration. A reading count (option C) does not show when events occurred, and adjacent readings are not independent. The lowest value (option D) shows the best moment, not the worst. Course convention: worked example, calculating improvement without overstating causation.

checks.prompt: What should determine when downstream observations become eligible after a fictional upstream treatment change?
choices: The start of the next shift, applied equally to each monitoring location.
The time when the chemical feed display first confirms the change.
The first downstream reading that favours the candidate, once it appears in the record.
The site's documented process response and appropriate hydraulic assessment.
checks.explanation: Eligibility follows the site's documented process response and hydraulic assessment. A fixed shift start (option A) ignores differences in travel time between monitoring points. The feed display (option C) shows the setting, not arrival at downstream points. Choosing the first favourable reading (option D) is selection bias. Course convention: eligibility rules in this module, consistent with Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario) on hydraulic basis.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case, supplied assumptions: a stream delivers 1,200 m³ at 10 mg/L suspended solids, then 800 m³ at 30 mg/L. Each concentration represents its entire interval. What suspended-solids mass passes during the combined interval?
choices: 36 kg of suspended solids.
18 kg of suspended solids for the interval.
24 kg of solids.
40 kg of suspended solids in total.
finalAssessment.explanation: Interval masses are 1,200 × 10 ÷ 1,000 = 12 kg and 800 × 30 ÷ 1,000 = 24 kg, totalling 36 kg. The 18 kg answer halves the total. The 24 kg answer counts only the 800 m³ interval. The 40 kg answer averages the concentrations to 20 mg/L and applies that to 2,000 m³, ignoring unequal volumes. Source: sp6 section 5.5.1, Mass Balance (p. 102).

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case, supplied daily assumptions: plant input is 5,000 m³, finished output 5,100 m³, waste output 80 m³, and storage falls 200 m³. An internal recycle moves 100 m³. What is the whole-plant unexplained residual?
choices: −380 m³ remains as the unexplained whole-plant balance residual.
20 m³ remains as the unexplained balance residual.
120 m³ remains as the unexplained balance residual.
−180 m³ remains as an unexplained residual.
finalAssessment.explanation: Storage falls by 200 m³, so the residual is 5,000 − 5,100 − 80 + 200 = 20 m³. The 120 m³ answer adds the internal recycle as new input. The −180 m³ answer omits the storage change. The −380 m³ answer applies the storage fall with the wrong sign. Source: sp6 section 5.5.1, Mass Balance (p. 102); the boundary rule is a course convention.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case, supplied assumptions: a downstream analyser displays a result at 11:20. Sample transport takes 6 min; upstream-to-downstream water travel takes 24 min. Clocks agree and no other lag applies. Which upstream passage time corresponds to this result?
choices: 11:14 at the upstream sampling location for this result.
10:44 at the upstream tap.
10:50 at the upstream sampling location.
10:56 at the upstream sampling location.
finalAssessment.explanation: Subtract sample transport (6 min) from 11:20 to reach downstream process passage at 11:14, then subtract 24 min of travel to reach 10:50 upstream. The 11:14 answer is downstream, not upstream. The 10:44 answer subtracts sample transport twice. The 10:56 answer subtracts travel only and omits sample transport. Course convention: alignment method in this module.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case, supplied assumptions: a displayed residual meets the local optimization target. The applicable validated procedure excludes the current contact configuration, and no supporting approval is documented. Which study conclusion is justified?
choices: Treat the target result as sufficient once a second residual reading confirms it.
Record target achievement and extend the earlier validation using unchanged nominal tank volume.
Treat the target result as evidence that validation extends to the current arrangement.
Record target achievement, but do not infer that the validated requirement is satisfied.
finalAssessment.explanation: Meeting an optimization target does not establish a validated requirement outside the supported configuration. A second residual reading (option A) cannot supply missing hydraulic validation. Extending earlier validation with nominal volume (option B) and treating the target as validation (option C) both assume the configuration is covered. Source: Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario), CT and T10 concepts.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case, supplied calculation assumptions: an inventory balance needs 6 kg of active ingredient. Product contains 25% active ingredient by mass and has density 1.20 kg/L. What product volume contains that mass? This is not an authorized feed quantity.
choices: 20 L of commercial product.
28.8 L of commercial product for the balance.
24 L of commercial product in total.
5 L of product.
finalAssessment.explanation: Active mass is 6 kg, so product mass is 6 ÷ 0.25 = 24 kg and volume is 24 ÷ 1.20 = 20 L. The 28.8 L answer multiplies product mass by density instead of dividing. The 24 L answer treats product mass as volume, which assumes a density of 1 kg/L. The 5 L answer divides active mass by density and ignores the 25% strength. Source: sp6 section 5.6.9.6, Calculating Percent Strength (p. 130).

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case, supplied assumptions: A and B each have 23 NTU. Alkalinity is 58 and 26 mg/L as CaCO3; temperatures are 12 and 4 °C, respectively. Each loses 18 mg/L as CaCO3 in a simplified balance. Which interpretation best sets test priorities?
choices: A retains 40 and B 8 mg/L as CaCO3; equal turbidity supports identical bench conditions.
A retains 40 and B 8 mg/L as CaCO3; B warrants buffering and cold-water checks.
A retains 76 and B 44 mg/L as CaCO3; B warrants buffering and cold-water checks.
A retains 40 and B 8 mg/L as CaCO3; both therefore have adequate buffering.
finalAssessment.explanation: Subtracting the 18 mg/L consumption gives 58 − 18 = 40 mg/L and 26 − 18 = 8 mg/L as CaCO3. B has less reserve and is colder, which supports targeted checks. The first option treats equal turbidity as equal chemistry. The third adds consumption instead of subtracting it. The fourth treats a remaining reserve as adequate without a criterion. Course convention: no minimum alkalinity is authorized in this module.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case, supplied assumptions: an intake event is stamped 10:06 by a clock running 6 min fast. Documented travel to the filter is 35 to 50 min for this configuration. All records use the same time zone. Which filter comparison window best matches the event?
choices: 10:00 to 10:15, after correcting the clock without adding travel.
10:29 to 10:44, after subtracting the clock offset again during alignment.
10:35 to 10:50, after correcting the clock and allowing for travel.
10:41 to 10:56, after using the stored timestamp and allowing for travel.
finalAssessment.explanation: The clock runs 6 min fast, so the corrected event time is 10:06 − 6 = 10:00. Adding the 35 to 50 min travel range gives 10:35 to 10:50. The 10:00 to 10:15 window omits travel. The 10:29 to 10:44 window applies the clock correction twice (09:54) before adding travel. The 10:41 to 10:56 window uses the uncorrected timestamp. Course convention: timing alignment in this module.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: paired intake samples have stable DOC but higher ultraviolet absorbance, with unchanged preparation and valid QC. Analysts propose changed organic character or increased total carbon. Which evidence package best separates these explanations?
choices: Repeat turbidity and apparent colour, then use agreement to infer a rise in total carbon.
Repeat DOC alone and use its stability to exclude any change in total organic carbon.
Compare historical feed rates and current absorbance, treating feed demand as a measure of total carbon.
Measure paired total organic carbon and method-matched absorbance, retaining sample fractions.
finalAssessment.explanation: Paired total organic carbon with method-matched absorbance keeps the fractions separate. Repeating turbidity and apparent colour (option A) measures neither total carbon nor organic character directly. Stable DOC alone (option B) cannot exclude change outside the DOC fraction. Feed demand (option C) reflects chemical requirement, not carbon content. Source: WQC Handbook, section 6.2 (TOC and DOC apparatus).

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: a raw-water trend spikes just after maintenance, while matched grabs remain steady. A brief source pulse and changed signal processing remain possible. Which review best distinguishes them?
choices: Compare original analyser output, processing settings, QC records and precise grab timing.
Compare the maintenance log with the displayed spike and attribute the spike to maintenance.
Compare the grab average with the trend maximum and retain whichever dataset has more readings.
Compare the daily mean with the previous day and accept a source pulse if the mean increased.
finalAssessment.explanation: Original analyser output, processing settings, QC records and grab timing show whether a missed pulse or a processing artefact explains the spike. Matching a maintenance date to the spike (option B) shows only coincidence. Comparing a grab average with a trend maximum and keeping the larger dataset (option C) counts readings rather than validity. A higher daily mean (option D) can hide a brief pulse. Source: US EPA 815-B-19-010, US technical guidance, not Ontario law.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: the current intake is cold, low in alkalinity and DOC-rich, with a fixed source blend. Archived periods all have similar turbidity. Which period offers the most defensible source-characterisation comparison?
choices: A cold period with matching alkalinity, changed blending and an overall daily DOC mean alone.
A cold period with matching alkalinity, DOC, blending and comparable analytical methods.
A cold period with matching DOC and blending, but higher alkalinity and a matching chemical-feed trend.
A period with matching temperature and alkalinity, but undocumented analytical methods and no DOC record.
finalAssessment.explanation: The selected period matches the relevant source properties, configuration and analytical basis. Option A uses a daily mean across a blend change, which hides the event. Option C matches DOC but not alkalinity, so buffering is not comparable. Option D matches temperature and alkalinity but has no DOC record and no documented methods, so it cannot support the profile. Similar turbidity or chemical-feed history does not establish a comparable source profile. Course convention: input-register matching.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: matched interval totals are 18.0 L of coagulant and 300 m³ of water. Density is 1.25 kg/L and strength is 8.00% by mass as Al₂O₃ equivalent. What interval active dose follows from these totals?
choices: 75 mg/L as Al₂O₃ equivalent.
0.600 mg/L as Al₂O₃ equivalent.
6.00 mg/L as Al₂O₃ equivalent.
60.0 mg/L as Al₂O₃ equivalent.
finalAssessment.explanation: Active mass is 18.0 L × 1.25 kg/L × 0.0800 = 1.80 kg. Dividing by 300 m³ gives 6.00 mg/L as Al₂O₃ equivalent. The 75 mg/L answer is the product-mass dose (22.5 kg ÷ 300 m³) and omits the 8% strength. The 0.600 mg/L answer divides by 3,000 m³. The 60.0 mg/L answer divides by 30 m³. Source: sp6 section 5.7.7.1, Chemical Feed Rate (p. 161).

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: at constant water flow, an old product feeds at 8.00 L/h, density 1.20 kg/L and 12.0% by mass as Al₂O₃ equivalent. A replacement has density 1.25 kg/L and 10.0% on the same basis. Which calculated feed preserves active dose, rounded to 0.01 L/h?
choices: 9.6 L/h of replacement product.
8.000 L/h of replacement product.
7.68 L/h of replacement product.
9.22 L/h of replacement product.
finalAssessment.explanation: The old active rate is 8.00 × 1.20 × 0.120 = 1.152 kg/h. The replacement supplies 1.25 × 0.100 = 0.125 kg/L, so 1.152 ÷ 0.125 = 9.216, or 9.22 L/h. The 9.6 L/h answer uses the old density with the new strength. The 8.000 L/h answer keeps the volumetric feed and ignores strength. The 7.68 L/h answer uses the new density with the old strength. This is an accounting comparison, not an authorized setting. Source: sp6 section 5.7.7.1 (p. 161).

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied screen, for this item only: mean ≤0.60 NTU, range ≤0.08 NTU, every pH 6.6 to 7.0. X: turbidity 0.48/0.60 NTU, pH 6.8/6.9. Y: turbidity 0.55/0.59 NTU, pH 6.7/6.8. Which conclusion follows?
choices: Just Y meets the screen because X exceeds the turbidity range criterion.
Just X meets the screen because its lower mean establishes better consistency.
Both meet the screen because each mean and each pH meet their criteria.
Neither meets the screen because both turbidity pairs show variation.
finalAssessment.explanation: X has mean 0.54 NTU but a range of 0.12 NTU, which fails this item's range limit. Y has mean 0.57 NTU, range 0.04 NTU and pH within 6.6 to 7.0, so only Y meets the screen. Option B selects X for its lower mean and ignores consistency. Option C ignores the range check. Option D wrongly rejects Y, whose range is within 0.08 NTU. Course convention: this item's own teaching screen.

finalAssessment.prompt: In a fictional study, candidate jars outperform baseline jars, but the candidate jars received a different settling time. Instrument checks passed. What evidence plan best addresses whether dose caused the improvement?
choices: Compare the existing averages and retain the condition with lower turbidity.
Repeat independent jars with matched settling and other bench conditions.
Treat the candidate as the only variable because instrument checks passed.
Repeat readings of the stored samples to narrow instrument uncertainty.
finalAssessment.explanation: Different settling times confound the dose comparison, so independent preparations under matched conditions are needed. Comparing averages (option A) keeps the confound. Treating the candidate as the only variable (option C) ignores the settling difference, and passing instrument checks does not remove it. Re-reading stored samples (option D) measures repeatability only. Source: sp6 glossary, Jar test; course convention on matched bench conditions.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional study has verified product strength, measured delivery and repeatable candidate performance. Downstream response remains uncertain. Which proposed trial package best supports site review without treating the bench result as authorization?
choices: Site-reviewed dose bounds and a closing summary using routine downstream records.
A candidate dose, routine sampling, and trial completion whenever average turbidity improves.
Site-approved bounds, matched monitoring, downstream checks, stop/revert criteria and review.
A candidate dose, enhanced settled-water checks, and wider changes if the trend remains favourable.
finalAssessment.explanation: A bounded proposal needs site-reviewed dose limits, matched monitoring, downstream checks, stop and revert criteria, and review. Option A has dose bounds and a summary, but no stop or revert rule. Option B continues while routine sampling and turbidity improve, with no defined stop. Option D expands the change if the trend stays favourable, which is not a review. Bench success supports review but does not authorize a plant change. Course convention: proposal content in this module.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional study assumptions: active areas A = 20 m², B = 30 m². Stable filtration flows change from A/B = 100/240 to 160/180 m³/h at matched run stages. Which loading summary is supported, without judging acceptability?
choices: Afterwards, A = 8.0 m/h and B = 6.0 m/h; aggregate rises to 7.0 m/h overall.
Afterwards, A = 5.0 m/h and B = 8.0 m/h; aggregate is 6.8 m/h.
Afterwards, A = 6.0 m/h and B = 8.0 m/h; aggregate remains at 6.8 m/h overall.
Afterwards, A = 8.0 m/h and B = 6.0 m/h; aggregate stays at 6.8 m/h.
finalAssessment.explanation: The new unit loadings are 160 ÷ 20 = 8.0 m/h and 180 ÷ 30 = 6.0 m/h. Total flow stays at 340 m³/h over 50 m², giving 6.8 m/h. The 7.0 m/h aggregate in option A is an unweighted average of the two loadings, which ignores unequal areas. Option B reports the pre-change unit loadings (100 ÷ 20 = 5.0 and 240 ÷ 30 = 8.0). Option C swaps the two unit loadings. Source: sp6 section 5.6.8.2, Filtration Rate (p. 120).

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional study assumptions: at run ages 3–7 h, A's headloss rises from 0.40 to 1.00 m and B's from 0.60 to 1.40 m. Both have stable loading of 5.0 m/h and valid, equivalent instruments. What are their average headloss accumulation rates and difference?
choices: A: 0.15 m/h; B: 0.20 m/h; difference: 0.05 m/h.
A: 0.25 m/h; B: 0.35 m/h; difference: 0.10 m/h.
A: 0.086 m/h; B: 0.114 m/h; difference: 0.028 m/h.
finalAssessment.explanation: The common interval is 7 − 3 = 4 h. A accumulates (1.00 − 0.40) ÷ 4 = 0.15 m/h and B accumulates (1.40 − 0.60) ÷ 4 = 0.20 m/h. Option B reports the headloss increase without dividing by duration. Option C divides endpoint headloss by duration, which includes headloss already present at run age 3 h. Option D divides the increase by elapsed run age (7 h) instead of the 4 h comparison duration. Source: sp6 section 5.6.8.2 (p. 120).

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional study records: clarified-water turbidity rises before both filters respond, allowing for verified travel times. After upstream recovery, only B remains elevated. Loading and run stage are matched; analyzers are valid. Which interpretation best fits?
choices: B's persistent response proves a bed defect caused both filters' initial rise.
A shared initial influence is supported; B's persistence needs unit-specific review.
The shared initial rise establishes that B has no filter-specific issue to investigate.
Matching loading establishes that the upstream event explains B's full response.
finalAssessment.explanation: The sequence supports a shared initial influence, while B's persistence under matched conditions warrants unit-specific review. Option A treats one filter's persistence as proof of a bed defect, which the data do not show. Option C says B has no issue to investigate, which reverses the evidence. Option D says matched loading explains the full response, but matched loading does not rule out a later, separate cause. Course convention: individual-filter approach in this module.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional study assumptions: valid 10 s turbidity records contain a 40 s rise during steady filtration. A proposed report retains only 15 min means. Which study record best preserves evidence for later review?
choices: Keep interval means and the maximum value, and omit event timing and state changes once the peak has been recorded for the report.
Keep the event plot and interval means, and discard the source records after checking that the plot image looks consistent with them.
Keep detailed records, flags and state changes; use interval means as additional context.
Keep detailed records only for the part of the event above the peak value, and retain interval means for all remaining periods of the run.
finalAssessment.explanation: Detailed records with flags and operating state preserve onset, duration, recovery and interpretability. Option A keeps a maximum and means, which lose duration and sequence. Option B keeps a plot but discards the records needed to check it. Option D keeps only the peak, losing the rise and recovery. Course convention: preserve short-duration changes rather than averaging them away.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional study assumptions: a turbidity rise appears 2 min before a flow step. Analyzer and flow clocks are unverified; nearby turbidity records carry a maintenance flag. What is the strongest next analytical step?
choices: Use the apparent event order to exclude the flow step, then examine upstream records.
Shift turbidity to follow the flow step, retaining the flagged values as process evidence.
Remove the flagged values permanently, then treat the remaining clock order as verified.
Retain original records, verify time bases and flags, then reassess the event sequence.
finalAssessment.explanation: Clock settings and flag meaning must be verified before event order is trusted, and originals must be kept. Option A uses an unverified apparent order to exclude the flow step. Option B shifts turbidity to match the flow step, which imposes a relationship. Option C deletes flagged values and treats unverified clocks as verified. Course convention: input-register checks in this module.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: working volume 480 m³, flow 360 m³/h, supported T10 factor 0.50 (dimensionless), endpoint free-chlorine residual 0.75 mg/L and condition-matched criterion 25 mg·min/L. With T10 = (volume/flow) × factor, which CT and ratio follow?
choices: CT is 30 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 1.20.
CT is 22.5 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 0.90.
CT is 60 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 2.4.
CT is 0.50 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 0.020.
finalAssessment.explanation: Flow is 360 ÷ 60 = 6 m³/min, nominal time is 480 ÷ 6 = 80 min, T10 is 40 min and CT is 0.75 × 40 = 30 mg·min/L. The ratio is 30 ÷ 25 = 1.20. The 22.5 mg·min/L answer uses 30 min as T10. The 60 mg·min/L answer uses nominal time (80 min) × 0.75, omitting the factor. The 0.50 answer uses the dimensionless factor as CT and divides by 25 to give 0.020. Source: sp6 section 5.6.9.3 (p. 126); Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario).

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: branch A has working volume 180 m³ and flow 360 m³/h. Combined branches have 600 m³ and 600 m³/h. Branch A's supported T10/nominal-time factor is 0.40 (dimensionless). Which nominal time and T10 apply to branch A?
choices: Nominal time is 30 min; T10 is 30 min.
Nominal time is 30 min; T10 is 12.0 min.
Nominal time is 18.0 min; T10 is 7.20 min.
Nominal time is 60.0 min; T10 is 24.0 min.
finalAssessment.explanation: Branch A flow is 360 ÷ 60 = 6 m³/min, so nominal time is 180 ÷ 6 = 30 min and T10 is 30 × 0.40 = 12 min. The 30 and 30 answer omits the factor. The 18.0 and 7.20 answer divides by 10 m³/min, the combined 600 m³/h flow. The 60.0 and 24.0 answer treats 180 m³/h as 3 m³/min. Source: sp6 section 5.6.7.2, Detention Time (p. 114); Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario).

finalAssessment.prompt: After level falls and flow rises, fictional supplied assumptions are volume 360 m³, flow 540 m³/h, endpoint free-chlorine residual 0.80 mg/L and condition-matched criterion 20 mg·min/L. T10 = (volume/flow) × 0.50 remains supported; the factor is dimensionless. Which result follows?
choices: CT is 0.267 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 0.0133.
CT is 20 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 1.00.
CT is 16 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 0.80.
CT is 32 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 1.6.
finalAssessment.explanation: Flow is 540 ÷ 60 = 9 m³/min, nominal time is 360 ÷ 9 = 40 min and T10 is 20 min. CT is 0.80 × 20 = 16 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 0.80. The 0.267 answer divides rather than multiplies. The 20 mg·min/L answer treats T10 as CT by omitting the residual. The 32 mg·min/L answer uses nominal time (40 min) instead of T10. Source: sp6 section 5.6.7.2 (p. 114).

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: a free-chlorine CT ratio was 1.30 at 15 °C and pH 7.0 (dimensionless). Temperature is now 5 °C and pH 8.0; residual and supported T10 are unchanged. No criterion for the new chemistry is supplied. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: The earlier ratio remains valid because residual and T10 are unchanged.
The earlier ratio is halved because the water temperature has fallen by 10 °C.
The earlier ratio can be corrected using the proportional temperature change alone.
The earlier ratio may not establish the comparison under the changed chemistry.
finalAssessment.explanation: The calculated C × T10 may be unchanged, but the applicable criterion must match the new temperature, pH, disinfectant and treatment objective. Option A reuses the old ratio without that check. Option B applies a fixed halving with no basis in the case. Option C applies a proportional correction that the case does not supply. Source: Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario); the case supplies no basis for a numerical correction.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: an endpoint analyser displays a residual at 10:06; sample transport takes 6 min. Clocks agree. The case-validated alignment method subtracts transport delay to select contemporaneous flow and level records. Which record time belongs with this residual?
choices: Use 10:00, accounting for sample transport.
Use 10:12, adding the sample transport delay.
Use 09:54, allowing twice for sample transport delay.
Use 10:06, matching the analyser display.
finalAssessment.explanation: Subtracting the 6 min transport delay from 10:06 gives 10:00 under the case's validated method. Adding the delay (10:12) pairs the residual with a later interval. Subtracting twice (09:54) double-counts the delay. Using the displayed time (10:06) pairs the residual with a later process interval than it represents. Source: sp6 section 5.6.9.3 (p. 126); the alignment method is a case assumption.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied case assumptions, not authorized values: eligible baseline turbidity is 0.90, 1.10 NTU; candidate is 0.72, 0.88 NTU. The primary criterion is at least 15% mean reduction. Disinfection review is incomplete. Which assessment is justified?
choices: The reduction is 25%; the primary criterion is met, but disinfection evidence still prevents an overall conclusion.
The reduction is 20%; the primary criterion is met, but full-barrier success remains unestablished.
The reduction is 10%; the primary criterion is missed and the candidate should be classified as ineffective.
The reduction is 20%; full-barrier success is established.
finalAssessment.explanation: The baseline mean is (0.90 + 1.10) ÷ 2 = 1.00 NTU and the candidate mean is 0.80 NTU, a 20% reduction, above the 15% criterion of this item. Dividing by the candidate mean gives 25%, which is the wrong denominator. The 10% answer divides the absolute reduction by the sum of the means. Reporting full-barrier success (option D) ignores the incomplete disinfection review. Course convention: primary-criterion arithmetic in this module.

finalAssessment.prompt: In a fictional authorized comparison, source turbidity falls as the candidate begins. Settled-water turbidity improves and stays improved after a planned return to baseline. Eligible windows and instrument checks are valid. Which interpretation is strongest?
choices: Treat the return result as proof that the candidate has a persistent benefit after withdrawal.
Reject the observed improvement because the source-water conditions changed during the comparison.
Report the improvement, identify the source trend, and seek a more comparable contrast.
Credit the candidate because improvement began during its use.
finalAssessment.explanation: The improvement is a valid observation, and its persistence after the planned return is consistent with a source-water trend rather than the candidate. Treating the return result as proof of persistent benefit (option A) overreads it. Rejecting the observed improvement (option B) discards valid data. Crediting the candidate because improvement began during its use (option D) mistakes timing for causation. Course convention: observation, association and causation are separated in this module.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional records show the primary outcome met. An individual filter crosses its trial-specific interruption criterion, although combined filtrate remains stable. The facility-approved trial plan requires interruption and escalation for that event. Which assessment fits?
choices: Recommend continuation because the combined result remains stable and the primary outcome was met on schedule, with no further review needed.
Classify as a full success because the primary outcome was met, and treat the filter event as a routine note.
Classify the trial as successful but record the filter event for discussion at the next routine review.
Record the primary benefit, reject overall success, and refer to the plan's interruption and escalation response.
finalAssessment.explanation: The primary outcome does not override an individual-filter protection criterion. Recommending continuation (option A) relies on a combined result that can hide a deteriorating filter. Calling it a full success (option B) and deferring the event to routine review (option C) ignore the approved response. Option D keeps the benefit, withholds overall success and points to the plan's response. Course convention: filter protection in the decision register.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional trial reaches its planned endpoint. Candidate readings look favourable, but a required analyser check failed and the plan provides no validated substitute. An extension is proposed solely to obtain a passing result. Which recommendation is defensible?
choices: Classify the comparison as inconclusive; retain the endpoint and require authorization and rationale for any extension.
Accept the favourable readings because failure of the analyser check does not itself establish that treatment performance deteriorated.
Discard flagged readings and continue collecting until the acceptance criterion is met.
Declare treatment failure and combine any extension readings with the original trial.
finalAssessment.explanation: Failed required quality checks make the evidence uninterpretable without proving treatment failure. Accepting favourable readings (option B) ignores the failed check. Discarding flagged readings and continuing until the criterion is met (option C) biases the comparison. Declaring failure and combining extension data with the original trial (option D) is unsupported and mixes unlike evidence. The original endpoint must remain identifiable. Course convention: extension rules in this module.

finalAssessment.prompt: In a fictional trial handover, settled-water results improve. Disinfectant residual is unchanged, but flow and contact configuration differ from baseline. What handover entry best supports a defensible cross-barrier review?
choices: Report unchanged residual as sufficient evidence of equivalent disinfection, with configuration details available on request if a reviewer asks for them.
Flag disinfection as unresolved; retain condition and hydraulic records, and identify review, escalation and reversion owners.
Omit disinfection from the handover because the trial concerns settled-water turbidity only.
Report improved turbidity and carry forward the previous CT assessment.
finalAssessment.explanation: Unchanged residual does not establish equivalent CT performance after flow or configuration changes, so disinfection is unresolved. Option A treats the residual as sufficient evidence. Option C omits disinfection altogether, although the trial changed flow and configuration. Option D carries forward a previous assessment that does not apply to the new configuration. Option B keeps the flag, the records and named owners. Source: Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario).
